title: Keycloak & On-Prem Ops
summary: Automate Keycloak via its admin REST API, validate OIDC config drift against Harbor, and build a health check script for your on-prem clusters. Directly useful for MD-2454 and the Kinetic-ID setup.

sections.title: Keycloak admin REST API
sections.body:
## Keycloak as a platform component: why it needs automation

Keycloak is an open-source identity and access management system that implements OpenID Connect (OIDC) and SAML. In a platform context, it is the central authority for who can log in to what: Harbor, ArgoCD, Grafana, internal tools, and developer-facing services can all delegate authentication to Keycloak rather than each maintaining their own user database. This single-sign-on (SSO) architecture is both more secure (fewer credential stores to compromise) and more convenient (one login for everything).

As platforms grow, Keycloak configuration becomes a source of drift. Realms accumulate clients, clients accumulate redirect URIs and roles, users accumulate group memberships. Changes are made through the UI, which leaves no audit trail and no way to reproduce the configuration if Keycloak needs to be rebuilt. Automating Keycloak management — creating clients, setting redirect URIs, managing groups — brings the same infrastructure-as-code discipline to identity that Terraform brings to cloud resources.

The Keycloak admin REST API is comprehensive. Everything visible in the Keycloak admin console is accessible via API: realms, clients, users, groups, roles, identity providers, client scopes. The API is secured by the same OIDC tokens Keycloak issues, which means your automation script must first authenticate to Keycloak to get a token before making admin calls.

The `client_credentials` grant type is the appropriate authentication method for service-to-service automation: no user is involved, and the script identifies itself using a client ID and client secret configured in Keycloak. The resulting access token is a JWT with a short expiry (typically 5 minutes for admin tokens), and for long-running scripts, token refresh logic may be needed — though for scripts that complete within a few minutes, a single token at startup is sufficient.

Keycloak has a full REST API. The admin client authenticates with client credentials or username/password.

```python
import requests
import os

class KeycloakAdmin:
    def __init__(self, base_url, realm, client_id, client_secret):
        self.base = base_url.rstrip("/")
        self.realm = realm
        self.session = requests.Session()
        self.session.headers["Content-Type"] = "application/json"
        self._token = None
        self._authenticate(client_id, client_secret)

    def _authenticate(self, client_id, client_secret):
        """Get admin access token using client credentials."""
        r = self.session.post(
            f"{self.base}/realms/{self.realm}/protocol/openid-connect/token",
            data={
                "grant_type": "client_credentials",
                "client_id": client_id,
                "client_secret": client_secret,
            },
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"},
            timeout=(5, 30),
        )
        r.raise_for_status()
        self._token = r.json()["access_token"]
        self.session.headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {self._token}"

    def get(self, path, **params):
        r = self.session.get(
            f"{self.base}/admin/realms/{self.realm}{path}",
            params=params, timeout=(5, 30)
        )
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r.json()

    def post(self, path, body):
        r = self.session.post(
            f"{self.base}/admin/realms/{self.realm}{path}",
            json=body, timeout=(5, 30)
        )
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r

    def put(self, path, body):
        r = self.session.put(
            f"{self.base}/admin/realms/{self.realm}{path}",
            json=body, timeout=(5, 30)
        )
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r

# Usage
kc = KeycloakAdmin(
    base_url=os.environ["KEYCLOAK_URL"],
    realm="master",
    client_id="admin-cli",
    client_secret=os.environ["KEYCLOAK_SECRET"],
)

# List clients
clients = kc.get("/clients")
for c in clients:
    print(f"  {c['clientId']:<30} protocol={c.get('protocol','?')} enabled={c['enabled']}")

# List users
users = kc.get("/users", max=100)
for u in users:
    print(f"  {u['username']:<30} email={u.get('email', '?')}")

# Get client by ID
harbor_client = kc.get("/clients", clientId="harbor")
```

sections.title: Detecting OIDC config drift between Keycloak and Harbor
sections.body:
## OIDC configuration drift: how integration configs break silently

When you wire Harbor to authenticate through Keycloak, both systems must agree on several values: the issuer URL (which Keycloak realm to use), the client ID (how Harbor identifies itself to Keycloak), the redirect URI (where Keycloak sends users after login), and the scopes requested during the flow. If any of these disagree, login fails — but the error message is often unhelpful, pointing to "invalid client" or "redirect_uri mismatch" without indicating which value is wrong or which system has the stale configuration.

Configuration drift happens when changes are made to one side without updating the other. A Keycloak realm is renamed during a reorganization; Harbor still has the old realm in its OIDC endpoint URL and login breaks. A Harbor redirect URI is updated but the old value was not removed from the Keycloak client's allowed list. A required OIDC scope (`groups`) is added to Harbor's config but never added to the Keycloak client's scope mappings.

The solution is automated validation that reads the configuration from both systems and compares them. This script does exactly that: it queries Harbor's configuration API, reads Keycloak's OIDC discovery endpoint, checks that they agree, and returns a list of discrepancies. Run this in CI after any Keycloak or Harbor configuration change to catch drift before users report broken logins.

The Keycloak discovery endpoint (`.well-known/openid-configuration`) is a standard OIDC mechanism — every compliant OIDC provider exposes it. It returns the issuer URL, the token endpoint, the authorization endpoint, and the supported scopes. Your validation script can use this to verify that Harbor's configured endpoint URL actually resolves to the expected Keycloak realm, without requiring any admin credentials for Keycloak itself.

Your MD-2454 work involves wiring Keycloak OIDC into Harbor. This script validates the config is correct on both sides.

```python
import requests
import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class OIDCConfig:
    provider_url:   str
    client_id:      str
    scope:          str
    admin_group:    Optional[str] = None
    auto_onboard:   bool = True
    verify_cert:    bool = True


def get_harbor_oidc_config(harbor_url, auth) -> OIDCConfig:
    """Read Harbor's OIDC config from the API."""
    r = requests.get(
        f"{harbor_url}/api/v2.0/configurations",
        auth=auth, timeout=(5, 30)
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    cfg = r.json()
    return OIDCConfig(
        provider_url  = cfg.get("oidc_endpoint", {}).get("value", ""),
        client_id     = cfg.get("oidc_client_id", {}).get("value", ""),
        scope         = cfg.get("oidc_scope", {}).get("value", ""),
        admin_group   = cfg.get("oidc_admin_group", {}).get("value"),
        auto_onboard  = cfg.get("oidc_auto_onboard", {}).get("value", True),
        verify_cert   = cfg.get("oidc_verify_cert", {}).get("value", True),
    )


def get_keycloak_oidc_metadata(keycloak_url, realm) -> dict:
    """Read Keycloak's OIDC discovery endpoint."""
    r = requests.get(
        f"{keycloak_url}/realms/{realm}/.well-known/openid-configuration",
        timeout=(5, 30)
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()


def check_harbor_client_exists(kc: 'KeycloakAdmin', client_id: str) -> bool:
    """Verify the Harbor client exists in Keycloak."""
    clients = kc.get("/clients", clientId=client_id)
    return len(clients) > 0


def validate_oidc_config(
    harbor_url,  harbor_auth,
    keycloak_url, keycloak_realm,
    expected_client_id="harbor",
) -> list[str]:  # returns list of issues
    issues = []

    harbor_cfg  = get_harbor_oidc_config(harbor_url, harbor_auth)
    kc_meta     = get_keycloak_oidc_metadata(keycloak_url, keycloak_realm)

    expected_provider = f"{keycloak_url}/realms/{keycloak_realm}"

    # Check 1: Harbor points to the right Keycloak realm
    if harbor_cfg.provider_url.rstrip("/") != expected_provider.rstrip("/"):
        issues.append(
            f"Provider URL mismatch:\n"
            f"  Harbor has:    {harbor_cfg.provider_url}\n"
            f"  Expected:      {expected_provider}"
        )

    # Check 2: Client ID matches
    if harbor_cfg.client_id != expected_client_id:
        issues.append(f"Client ID mismatch: Harbor={harbor_cfg.client_id}, expected={expected_client_id}")

    # Check 3: Required scopes present
    scopes = set(harbor_cfg.scope.split())
    required = {"openid", "profile", "email"}
    missing = required - scopes
    if missing:
        issues.append(f"Missing OIDC scopes: {missing}")

    return issues


# Run validation
issues = validate_oidc_config(
    harbor_url="https://harbor.example.com",
    harbor_auth=("admin", "harbor_password"),
    keycloak_url="https://keycloak.example.com",
    keycloak_realm="platform",
)

if not issues:
    print("✓ Keycloak/Harbor OIDC config is consistent")
else:
    print("✗ Config drift detected:")
    for issue in issues:
        print(f"  - {issue}")
    sys.exit(1)
```

sections.title: On-prem cluster health check script
sections.body:
## On-premises cluster health checks: different constraints from managed Kubernetes

On-premises Kubernetes clusters (MicroK8s, k3s, kubeadm-built clusters) present different operational challenges than managed EKS or GKE. You are responsible for the control plane, the nodes, the network CNI, and the storage layer — none of which a cloud provider manages for you. Automated health checks are more critical here because there is no cloud provider console showing you that your API server is unreachable.

Health checks for on-prem clusters need to answer questions in layers. First: can you reach the cluster at all? (`cluster-info` failing often means the API server is down or your kubeconfig is wrong.) Second: are the nodes in a ready state, or are any in `NotReady`? (A node in `NotReady` means its pods may be evicted and rescheduled, which triggers cascading failures for stateful workloads.) Third: are critical system pods healthy? kube-system pods — coredns, kube-proxy, the CNI plugin — are the foundation everything else depends on.

The `subprocess`-based approach here is a pragmatic choice for a standalone health check script. It uses `kubectl` directly, which means it respects whatever context and kubeconfig the operator has configured, it works with any Kubernetes distribution, and it does not require the `kubernetes` Python library to be installed. The downside is that it is tied to the `kubectl` binary being present and configured — which is fine for a script meant to run from an operator's laptop or a bastion host, but less appropriate for a script running inside the cluster itself.

The `HealthResult` dataclass gives the check functions a consistent return type: every check returns the same structure, which the main `run_health_check()` function can handle uniformly without knowing the specifics of each check. Adding a new check is a matter of writing a function that returns `HealthResult` objects and adding a call to it in `run_health_check()`.

For your Kinetic-ID / MicroK8s clusters — a health check that can run from CI or a cron job.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""On-prem cluster health check — for MicroK8s / k3s environments."""

import subprocess
import json
import sys
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List

@dataclass
class HealthResult:
    component: str
    ok: bool
    message: str = ""
    details: dict = field(default_factory=dict)


def check_kubectl_access(context=None) -> HealthResult:
    args = ["kubectl", "cluster-info"]
    if context:
        args += ["--context", context]
    result = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=10)
    ok = result.returncode == 0
    return HealthResult(
        component="cluster-access",
        ok=ok,
        message=result.stdout.split("\n")[0] if ok else result.stderr.strip()
    )


def check_nodes(context=None) -> List[HealthResult]:
    args = ["kubectl", "get", "nodes", "-o", "json"]
    if context:
        args += ["--context", context]
    result = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=15)
    if result.returncode != 0:
        return [HealthResult("nodes", False, result.stderr.strip())]

    nodes = json.loads(result.stdout)["items"]
    results = []
    for node in nodes:
        name = node["metadata"]["name"]
        conditions = node["status"].get("conditions", [])
        ready = next((c for c in conditions if c["type"] == "Ready"), None)
        ok = ready and ready["status"] == "True"
        results.append(HealthResult(
            component=f"node/{name}",
            ok=ok,
            message=ready["message"] if ready else "No Ready condition"
        ))
    return results


def check_critical_pods(context=None, namespaces=("kube-system",)) -> List[HealthResult]:
    results = []
    for ns in namespaces:
        args = ["kubectl", "get", "pods", "-n", ns, "-o", "json"]
        if context: args += ["--context", context]
        result = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=15)
        if result.returncode != 0:
            results.append(HealthResult(f"pods/{ns}", False, result.stderr))
            continue
        pods = json.loads(result.stdout)["items"]
        for pod in pods:
            name = pod["metadata"]["name"]
            phase = pod["status"].get("phase", "Unknown")
            restarts = sum(
                cs.get("restartCount", 0)
                for cs in pod["status"].get("containerStatuses", [])
            )
            ok = phase == "Running" and restarts < 5
            if not ok:
                results.append(HealthResult(
                    component=f"pod/{ns}/{name}",
                    ok=False,
                    message=f"phase={phase} restarts={restarts}"
                ))
    return results


def run_health_check(context=None):
    results = []
    results.append(check_kubectl_access(context))
    results.extend(check_nodes(context))
    results.extend(check_critical_pods(context))

    passed = [r for r in results if r.ok]
    failed = [r for r in results if not r.ok]

    print(f"\n=== Cluster Health: {context or 'current'} ===")
    for r in failed:
        print(f"  [✗] {r.component}: {r.message}")
    print(f"\n{len(passed)}/{len(results)} checks passed")
    return len(failed) == 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ok = run_health_check()
    sys.exit(0 if ok else 1)
```

sections.title: Exercise: OIDC drift checker + cluster health in one tool
sections.body:
## Exercise: a unified operations check tool

The capstone of this lesson is combining the cluster health check and the OIDC drift check into a single tool with a consistent CLI interface. This is the final step in building a tool that could realistically be wired into a CI pipeline or run as a daily cron job.

The structural challenge is that the two checks operate on different systems (Kubernetes vs. Keycloak/Harbor REST APIs) and have different failure modes. The tool should return a non-zero exit code if any check fails, but it should always run all checks and report all failures — not stop at the first failure. An operator looking at a broken environment needs to see everything that is wrong, not discover problems one at a time.

For the `cluster-health` subcommand, the terminal exercises below will show you the raw data before you wrap it in Python — understanding the kubectl output format before automating it is always the right approach. For `oidc-check`, the sandbox uses mock services, so the validation will check against simulated Keycloak and Harbor endpoints.

This tool, when complete, represents the full arc of what you have built across weeks 7–12: Kubernetes API access, REST API clients, error handling, structured output, and proper CLI design — all applied to real operational problems.

Combine both into `ops_check.py` — a single tool with two subcommands:

```bash
python3 ops_check.py cluster-health
python3 ops_check.py oidc-check --harbor-url https://harbor.example.com
```

Try the cluster health part in the terminal now:

```bash
# Get all pods and flag the bad ones
kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] |
  select(.status.phase != "Running") |
  [.metadata.namespace, .metadata.name, .status.phase] | @tsv
'

# Check node status
kubectl get nodes -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] |
  .metadata.name as $name |
  .status.conditions[] |
  select(.type == "Ready") |
  [$name, .status, .message] | @tsv
'

# Simulate the full health check script
python3 << 'EOF'
import subprocess, json

result = subprocess.run(
    ['kubectl', 'get', 'pods', '-A', '-o', 'json'],
    capture_output=True, text=True
)
pods = json.loads(result.stdout)['items']
problems = [
    f"{p['metadata']['namespace']}/{p['metadata']['name']}: {p['status'].get('phase', '?')}"
    for p in pods
    if p['status'].get('phase') not in ('Running', 'Succeeded')
]
if problems:
    print('Issues found:')
    for p in problems: print(f'  ✗ {p}')
else:
    print('All pods healthy')
EOF
```

This is your capstone — combine everything from weeks 4–11 into one deployable tool.
